Pregnancy

Signs of Labor: How to Tell When It Is Really Starting

Updated: August 5, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

The clearest signs of labor are contractions that become regular, stronger, and closer together, your water breaking, and a blood-tinged discharge called bloody show. In the days before, you may also notice the baby dropping lower, the loss of your mucus plug, loose stools, or a burst of nesting energy. This guide walks through each sign, how to tell practice contractions from the real thing, and when to call your provider or head in.

Early clues in the days before labor

In the last weeks of pregnancy, your body often sends advance notices. One is lightening, when the baby settles lower into the pelvis. Breathing may feel easier while pelvic pressure and bathroom trips increase. In a first pregnancy this can happen two to four weeks before labor; in later pregnancies it may not happen until labor begins. Many people also notice a low, dull backache, cramps that feel like a period, or looser stools as the body releases hormones that soften the cervix. None of these signs starts a clock. They simply tell you that things are moving in the right direction.

You may also lose your mucus plug, the thick discharge that has sealed the cervix. It can come away all at once or in pieces over several days, and it is often tinged pink or brown. That tinge is called bloody show, and it usually means the cervix is softening and beginning to open. Bloody show is one of the better clues that labor is roughly 24 to 48 hours away, especially when it arrives alongside period-like cramps and loose stools, but it carries no guarantee: labor may follow within hours or still be days off, so treat it as a heads-up rather than a starting gun. A sudden burst of energy to clean and organize, often called nesting, is common around this time too. Bright red bleeding is different and deserves a call to your provider.

Braxton Hicks or the real thing

Braxton Hicks contractions are practice tightenings, and they follow a recognizable pattern of their own. They show up irregularly, do not get closer together, and do not grow stronger over time. Most people feel them only in the front of the belly, as a tightening that is uncomfortable rather than truly painful. The most useful test is to change what you are doing. Walk if you have been resting, lie down on your left side if you have been active, drink a large glass of water, or soak in a warm bath. Braxton Hicks contractions usually fade with one of these changes, especially in the weeks before your due date.

True labor contractions keep coming no matter what you do. They settle into a rhythm, arrive at roughly regular intervals, and those intervals gradually shorten. Each contraction also lasts longer and feels stronger than the ones before it. Many people describe a wave that starts in the lower back and wraps around to the front, or a deep menstrual cramp that peaks and then releases. A practical benchmark: when you have to stop walking or talking to breathe through a contraction, it is doing real work. If a warm bath, water, and rest have not slowed the pattern within an hour or so, you are likely watching early labor unfold.

What early contractions feel like and how to time them

At first, real contractions rarely feel dramatic. Common descriptions include strong period cramps low in the belly, a dull ache in the lower back that comes and goes in waves, or pressure in the pelvis and thighs. In early labor, contractions are often 10 to 20 minutes apart and last around 30 to 45 seconds. Over hours they typically move closer together and stretch toward a minute. Everyone's experience differs; some people feel mostly back pain, and some barely notice early contractions at all. What matters is not how any single contraction feels, but whether the overall pattern is building.

Timing removes the guesswork. Measure frequency from the start of one contraction to the start of the next, and duration from the start of a contraction to its end. Time them for about an hour, then rest; there is no need to log every contraction all night. Jot the times in BeMama or on paper so you can read the pattern back to your provider instead of estimating from memory. While you time, keep life gentle: eat something light, sip fluids, empty your bladder, and rest between waves. Early labor can last many hours, and saving energy now is one of the most useful things you can do.

If your water breaks

Movies suggest labor always begins with a dramatic gush, but only about 1 in 10 labors actually starts with the water breaking. For most people, contractions come first and the water breaks later, sometimes not until well into active labor. When it does happen, it can be a sudden gush or a slow, steady trickle that is easy to mistake for leaking urine. Amniotic fluid is usually clear or pale straw colored, with little or no smell, and it keeps coming even after you empty your bladder. If you are unsure, put on a clean pad and check it again after 30 minutes or so.

If you think your water has broken, note four things before you call: the time it happened, the color of the fluid, any odor, and roughly how much there was. Then call your provider even if you feel fine and have no contractions, because once the sac is open the team will want a plan for reducing infection risk. Do not put anything in the vagina, including tampons, and skip baths until you have spoken with someone. Fluid that looks green or brown, or has a foul smell, needs an immediate call, as does any heavy bleeding along with it.

When to head in, and when to call right away

For a first baby with an uncomplicated pregnancy, many providers suggest the 5-1-1 rule of thumb: call or head in when contractions are about five minutes apart, last about one minute each, and have kept that pattern for one hour. Treat it as a starting point, not a universal rule. Your own provider may set a different threshold, and it is worth asking at a late-pregnancy visit exactly when they want to hear from you. Second and later labors often move faster, so the bar is usually earlier. If you tested positive for group B strep, you may be asked to come in as soon as labor starts or your water breaks.

Some signs skip the timing rules entirely. Call your provider or go in right away for bright red bleeding heavier than spotting, regular contractions or leaking fluid before 37 weeks, fluid that is green or brown, a noticeable drop in your baby's movements, constant severe pain, or fever. And call whenever you simply feel that something is wrong; that instinct is a legitimate reason. No article can weigh your history, your exam findings, or your baby's pattern the way your own care team can. Labor triage lines answer these calls all day and night, and no one will mind if the answer turns out to be Braxton Hicks.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Birth preferences are most useful as a flexible conversation about priorities, pain relief, support, newborn care, and what may change if safety concerns arise. Labor signs and the timing for hospital assessment should follow instructions from the local maternity service.

Induction and cesarean birth are clinical decisions with benefits, risks, and alternatives that depend on gestational age and the health of the pregnant person and fetus. Ask what is recommended, why, what alternatives exist, and what to expect during recovery.

How BeMama can help

Use BeMama to prepare questions, preferences, hospital details, and the instructions your maternity team provides. It cannot diagnose labor or determine the safest mode or timing of birth.

When to seek help

Contact maternity care for regular painful contractions as instructed, ruptured membranes, bleeding, reduced fetal movement, severe pain, or any urgent concern.

Key takeaways

  • True labor contractions get longer, stronger, and closer together no matter what you do.
  • Losing your mucus plug or seeing bloody show means labor is near, but it may still be hours or days away.
  • Only about 1 in 10 labors begins with the water breaking; note the time, color, odor, and amount, then call.
  • The 5-1-1 pattern is a common cue to head in, but follow the threshold your own provider gives you.
  • Call right away for bleeding, fluid or regular contractions before 37 weeks, green fluid, or reduced movement.

Frequently asked questions

How do I know if I am in labor?

You are likely in labor when contractions arrive at regular intervals, get stronger and closer together over an hour or more, and keep going no matter how you rest or move. Braxton Hicks contractions, by contrast, stay irregular and usually fade with a change of position, fluids, or a warm bath. Water breaking or bloody show alongside a building contraction pattern makes labor even more likely. When in doubt, call your provider and describe what you are feeling.

What is the difference between Braxton Hicks and real contractions?

Braxton Hicks contractions are irregular, stay about the same strength, are felt mostly in the front of the belly, and usually ease with movement, water, or a warm bath. Real labor contractions form a rhythm: they come at shrinking intervals, last longer, feel stronger each time, and continue no matter what you do. Many people feel true contractions start in the back and wrap around to the front. An hour of timing usually makes the difference clear.

How do I know if my water broke?

Broken water is usually a gush or a continuous trickle of clear or pale straw colored fluid that keeps coming even after you empty your bladder. Urine tends to be yellowish and stops, while amniotic fluid has little or no odor and does not. Put on a clean pad, note the time, color, odor, and amount, then call your provider even if nothing else is happening. Green or brown fluid, or a foul smell, needs an immediate call.

When should I go to the hospital for contractions?

A common rule of thumb for a first baby is 5-1-1: go in when contractions are about five minutes apart, last about one minute, and have held that pattern for one hour. Your provider may give you a different threshold, and second labors, a long drive, group B strep, or any complication can move it earlier. Go regardless of timing for bleeding, fluid or regular contractions before 37 weeks, green fluid, or reduced movement.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
